p: LingoLLM is a self-hosted tool for learning languages with large language models. For every language you learn you keep a language profile, and everything you practise belongs to it.

It runs in your browser - as a desktop app on your own computer, or as a small server for you and your friends - and works with any OpenAI-compatible API: OpenAI, OpenRouter, LiteLLM, llama.cpp, LM Studio, Ollama, vLLM, and others.
The platform and the language profiles are in place, the chat and lesson screens are not. See the TODO for what is planned.
Language profiles - several profiles, also of the same language, switched from the Learning tab. See Language profiles.
Any OpenAI-compatible model - including reasoning models, with per-model limits. A shared model can be limited per user. See Inference providers.
Multiple users - each with their own profiles and models; administrators manage users, backups, and cleanup. See Administration.
Backups and trash - scheduled database backups, and a trash from which deleted objects can be restored. See Database backups and Trash.
Languages of the interface - every user picks their own. See Account & settings.
Extensions - plugins add features at runtime. See Extensions.

Installation

LingoLLM has no model of its own. It needs an OpenAI-compatible API to write text: a cloud service (OpenAI, OpenRouter...) or a model running on your own computer (llama.cpp, LM Studio, Ollama, vLLM...). Have the API address and an API key (if the service needs one) ready.
LingoLLM runs in your browser. You can install it in two ways:
One person on one computer
Port 8080, normally behind a reverse proxy with HTTPS
Server (Docker)
Several users, or access from other devices

The portable launcher accepts these options:
With --host 0.0.0.0 (or another address) LingoLLM is reachable from your network over plain HTTP. For access from other devices use the server behind HTTPS instead.

p: Quit LingoLLM, replace the app (or the portable folder) with the new version and start it again. Your data stays in .lingollm and is upgraded automatically on the first start; before the structure of the database changes, LingoLLM saves a copy of it in db-backups. Extensions are built for one LingoLLM version, so update them at the same time (see Managing extensions).
Delete the app or the folder. To remove your data as well, delete the .lingollm folder.
Run LingoLLM as a server when several people use it, or when you want to open it from other devices. Every user gets their own language profiles and inference providers.
Docker with Docker Compose
About 512 MB of memory for LingoLLM
For access over the internet: a domain and a reverse proxy with HTTPS (see below)

The first docker compose up builds the image from source, which takes a few minutes. LingoLLM then listens on port 8080. Open http://server:8080 and create the administrator account (see First start).

c:
git clone https://github.com/Enerccio/LingoLLM.git
cd LingoLLM
docker compose up -d

p: Instead of building from source you can use the image published with each release (linux/amd64 and linux/arm64). In docker-compose.yml, replace the build: block with image::
latest is the newest release, edge the development version, and 1.1.0 (or 1.1) pins a release. The rest of the file stays the same.

c:
services:
  lingollm:
    image: ghcr.io/enerccio/lingollm:latest

p: Everything is set in docker-compose.yml:
Setting
What it does
ports
8080:8080 publishes LingoLLM on port 8080 of the host. Use 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 when only a reverse proxy on the same host should reach it.
volumes

./data holds the database, backups and extensions. Keep it, and include it in your server backups. It is created on the first start if it doesn't exist; on start the container makes it owned by the user LingoLLM runs as inside the container (jetty), so the files in it belong to that user's ID on the host.
-Xmx512m
Maximum memory. Raise it (for example -Xmx1g) for many users or many large chats.
After changing the file, apply it with docker compose up -d.

c:
services:
  lingollm:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    container_name: lingollm-app
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    volumes:
      - ./data:/var/lingollm/.lingollm
    environment:
      - JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-Duser.home=/var/lingollm -Xms256m -Xmx512m -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/lingollm/.lingollm/heapdump.hprof

p: Passwords and login cookies are sent with every request. Over plain HTTP anyone on the way can read them. Put LingoLLM behind a reverse proxy with HTTPS.
The Save login option on the login screen also needs HTTPS: its cookies are marked secure, so browsers keep them only on HTTPS connections.
LingoLLM updates the page over a WebSocket connection, so the proxy must forward WebSocket upgrades. Examples for lingollm.example.com:
Caddy gets the certificate and forwards WebSockets automatically.

Failed logins are throttled per user and per client address (after 30 failures from one address, logins from it are refused for a growing time, up to 15 minutes). LingoLLM only believes the X-Forwarded-For header of a proxy you name: without it, all users appear to come from the proxy's address and 30 failures from anyone block everybody for a while. Keep the header in the proxy configuration (as above) and add -DtrustedProxies=address or range of the proxy to JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS in docker-compose.yml. A proxy on the Docker host reaches the container from the Docker network, normally 172.16.0.0/12; several entries are separated by commas. The throttling is kept in memory, restarting LingoLLM clears it.
c: lingollm.example.com { reverse_proxy localhost:8080 }

server { listen 443 ssl; server_name lingollm.example.com; ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/lingollm.example.com/fullchain.pem; ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/lingollm.example.com/privkey.pem; client_max_body_size 100m; # uploads of backups and extensions location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080; proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade; proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade"; proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; proxy_read_timeout 1h; # long requests keep the connection open } }

p: Inside the container, localhost is the container itself, not the server. To use a model server that runs on the Docker host (llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio...), use the address http://host.docker.internal:port/v1 in the inference provider. On Linux, add this to the service in docker-compose.yml:
The model server must also listen on an address the container can reach, not only on 127.0.0.1.

c:
extra_hosts:
      - "host.docker.internal:host-gateway"

p: With the prebuilt image use docker compose pull and docker compose up -d instead.
The database is upgraded automatically when the new version starts. LingoLLM saves a copy of the database before it changes its structure, but make a database backup of your own first as well.

c:
git pull
docker compose up -d --build

p: rebuild.sh (Linux, macOS) and rebuild.bat (Windows) in the repository root do the update for you; run them from the root, for example from a cron job or a scheduled task. They fetch the remote branch and do nothing when there is nothing new (--force rebuilds and restarts anyway, for example after changing docker-compose.yml). Otherwise they stop the container, git pull, rebuild the bundled plugins and copy their JARs into data/extensions (replacing the installed ones), and start the container again with docker compose up -d --build. If any step fails, the script stops with a message.

The Docker image doesn't contain the extensions, and they have to be built from the same source as the application. You don't need Java or Maven for that: lingollm/plugins/docker-compose.yml builds all of them in a container, which builds the application first and then every plugin, and copies the JARs into lingollm/plugins/build:

The first build takes several minutes (it downloads the dependencies of the application). Then copy the JARs into data/extensions and restart LingoLLM, or load them in Admin → Extensions (see Extensions). rebuild.sh / rebuild.bat do the copying for you, so on a server that uses them the plugins are always updated together with the application.

c:
docker compose -f lingollm/plugins/docker-compose.yml build
docker compose -f lingollm/plugins/docker-compose.yml run --rm plugins

p: The image has a Docker health check: docker ps shows (health: starting) while LingoLLM starts (up to two minutes), then (healthy). It is unhealthy when port 8080 stops answering with a page. Docker does not restart an unhealthy container by itself; use the status for your monitoring or an auto-heal tool.

c: docker compose logs -f lingollm

LingoLLM has a layout made for phones. The phone layout is not a copy of the desktop one: it is simpler, a few things are missing and not every extension works in it. This page lists the differences.

l: When the phone layout is used
p: LingoLLM looks at the width of the browser window when the page loads. Narrower than 768 pixels gives you the phone layout, anything wider the normal workspace.
Tablets and phones in landscape mode are usually wider than 768 pixels and get the desktop layout.
The layout is not switched while you work. If you turn the phone or tablet on its side, or resize the window, the layout stays as it was until you reload the page.
A narrow desktop browser window gets the phone layout too, which is handy to try it.
Like the desktop, the phone layout can be added to the home screen like an app (Install app / Add to Home Screen in the browser menu).

The tabs on the left are replaced by a drawer. Tap the menu button in the top bar to open it, tap a tab to switch to it. The tab you are on fills the whole screen and its name is shown in the top bar.

The drawer has the same tabs as the desktop - Learning, Settings, Inference Providers, Resources and Trash - and below them the interface Language, Change Password and Logout. The Learning tab, with the language selector, is the same as on the desktop.
Differences from the desktop:
The Settings header stacks its buttons under the title. The settings and their extension panels are the same.
Inference Providers and Trash list each entry as text with the buttons next to it, instead of a wide table.

An administrator on a phone is a normal user: there is no Admin button. The administrator tasks have to be done in the desktop layout, that is in a window wider than 768 pixels (reload the page after widening it).

The phone layout has its own classes, so an extension has to support it explicitly. Extensions that don't may add nothing at all on the phone; they appear where their author made them work. If an extension seems to be missing, check it in the desktop layout. How an extension supports the phone is described in the developer manual.
If you need something that is missing on the phone, turn the phone on its side and reload, or open LingoLLM in a wider window; your profiles and settings are the same everywhere.
To reach LingoLLM from a phone it has to run as a server: the desktop app listens on your computer only.

When the API refuses a request, LingoLLM says what to fix instead of showing an internal error, followed by what the API itself said:
Wrong Model; use Refresh to see the names the API knows.
Wrong OpenAI URL; it usually ends with /v1.

Reasoning models think before they answer. With Enable Reasoning checked, LingoLLM sends the chosen Reasoning Effort (None, Low, Medium or High) to the API as reasoning_effort. More effort usually means better planned text, but slower and more expensive responses. Not every API supports the parameter; if requests fail with reasoning enabled, turn it off.
Reasoning counts toward the response: give reasoning models a larger Max Response Tokens, or the text may be cut off after a long reasoning.

On an installation with several users, an administrator can share a provider: check Shared with all users in the provider's dialog (the checkbox is only there for administrators). Every user then finds it in in their Inference Providers tab, marked Shared Yes. They can use it, but they can't open it, see its address or API key, change it or delete it; only its owner can.
Sharing a provider lets the other users spend the owner's quota with the service. To stop users from adding providers of their own, so that they can only use the shared ones, see Users and providers.

An administrator can limit what each user may do with a shared provider. In the Inference Providers tab, the administrator who owns a shared provider has a Limits button (a user with a lock) in its row, which opens a table with the limits that were set. Add limit creates a new one: pick the user and a limit type.
Limit type
Meaning
Unlimited
No limit (the same as having none).
Token limit
The user can use up to the given number of tokens per period.
Not available
The user can not use the provider; anything that would send a request to it fails.

A token limit has a reset (daily, weekly from Monday, or monthly; calendar periods in the time zone of the server) and three limits that can each be left empty for no limit: the tokens sent, the tokens generated, and both together (in total). Whichever is reached first stops the user until the next reset. If all three are set, the sent plus the generated limit must not be below the total (the total could then never be reached), otherwise the dialog refuses to save. For example a total of 100,000 with 100,000 sent and 20,000 generated is fine, a total of 100,000 with 20,000 sent and 10,000 generated is not.

Nothing is reset on a timer: the tokens used start from zero when the user uses the provider (or looks at their limits) for the first time in a new period. The size of a request is known before it is sent, so a request whose prompt would take the user over the sent or in total limit is refused (the prompt is measured with LingoLLM's own estimate, which can differ a little from the service's count). The tokens generated are not known in advance: they are counted when the request ends, so the user is stopped only once the limit is reached and the last response can go over it. Users without a limit in the table are not limited.

To keep the generated tokens from going over, check Hard limit (only available with a limit of the generated tokens). A request reserves room for the largest response it allows (the Max Response Size of the provider), and with a hard limit it is refused when that reserve does not fit into what is left of the generated limit. So a hard limit lower than the response size of the provider refuses every request; the table and the user's info show hard next to such a limit. The hard limit only covers the generated tokens, the in total limit can still be gone over by the last response.

Every user sees the shared providers in their tab as read-only rows. The info button (the circle with an i) of a shared provider shows their own limit: what they used in this period, the limits and when they reset. When a limit is reached, anything that would send a request to the provider shows an error instead.

The Inference Providers tab shows, per provider, the Tokens sent (the prompt, "prefill") and Tokens generated (the response, reasoning included) you have used with it. A shared provider has a count of its own for each user, so you see only your part. Administrators also get a Usage per user button on the tab, which opens a table with what every user has used of every provider (tokens sent, tokens generated, requests and the time of the last one).

The numbers are what the service reports; a service that doesn't report them (or a request that is stopped in the middle) is counted with a local estimate, so those numbers are approximate. A request that fails before any text arrived isn't counted, and neither is Test Connection. The numbers stay at zero until a screen that talks to the model (a chat, a lesson) is used. Unless an administrator has set a limit for you on a shared provider, the counts are only informational.

l: Objects that belong to other objects
p: Deleting an object deletes what belongs to it, and restoring it brings that back: a language profile takes its chats and their messages with it, a chat its messages, an inference provider its usage numbers. You don't need to tick them: restore the profile, and its chats come with it. They show up in the table as separate rows; restoring one of them alone only works when the object it belongs to is not deleted.

Some objects can't live without another object: a chat and a message need their language profile, a message needs its chat. An object whose profile or chat is deleted can only be restored together with it: tick both. If you tick only the message, LingoLLM restores nothing and tells you what is missing:
Nothing was restored. These objects need a deleted object that is not selected. Select it too, or leave them deleted.
Tick the object it names and restore again. Objects that are not deleted any more (restored in the meantime, or an object you didn't delete) are not a problem.

A message that was deleted from the middle of a chat had its following messages moved to its parent. Restoring it brings the message back under its parent as a new branch, without the messages that followed it: they stay where they were moved to. Restore the whole chat instead of single messages when you want it as it was.

Waiting for the cleanup is not always what you want: a message you know you never need again can be removed right away. Tick it and click Delete Permanently; LingoLLM asks first, and this can't be undone.

Only messages can be deleted permanently. The button is disabled while anything else is ticked: profiles, chats and the rest wait for the administrator's cleanup, so you can't remove a whole profile by accident.
Messages that are below a removed message are not removed with it, whether they are deleted or not: they move to its parent.
LingoLLM deletes nothing when something can't be removed (for example an extension still needs the object) and tells you which one.

LingoLLM keeps much of an object's data (the text of a message, the note of a profile, notes that extensions saved) as JSON next to it. Extended Content in a row shows it, so you can check what an object contains before you restore it, for example to find the right message. Objects without such data (resources) have no link; an object that has none shows This object has no extended content.

Administrators see the deleted objects of all users and can restore any of them. The User filter above the table shows the objects of one user; the User column tells whose they are. Restored objects go back to their owner.
The same table is in Admin → Cleanup (Trash), so you can see what the next cleanup removes. Objects of a deleted user can't be restored: they depend on the user.
Extensions add features to LingoLLM without changing the application itself. Extensions that come with LingoLLM are listed below; how to write one is described in the developer manual.
Extension
What it does
Gemma 4 tools fix
Function calls work with Gemma 4 models whose API expects the role tool_responses.

Extensions are installed by an administrator for the whole LingoLLM installation, in Admin → Extensions: they are JAR files, uploaded with Load Extension (.jar). See Managing extensions for the details.
Once installed, an extension is available to every user. An extension loaded while LingoLLM runs shows up in windows opened afterwards: reload the page to see it.

Extensions hook into the user interface of one LingoLLM version. An extension built for a different version may stop working or break parts of the application. Use the extensions that come with your version of LingoLLM.
The phone layout has its own classes, so an extension has to support it. Extensions are installed from the Admin page, which a phone doesn't have.

Extensions with settings add a section to Settings → Extension Settings (the second tab of the Settings page). These settings belong to your account, like the rest of Settings, and are saved with its Save button.
Extensions keep their data together with the data it belongs to, so it is included in database backups.
Uninstalling an extension doesn't delete its data: installing it again brings it back.
An extension can add a language of the interface (see Account & settings).
Makes function calling work with Gemma 4 models whose API expects another role for the results of the calls.

When the model calls a function, LingoLLM sends the result back to it in a message with the role tool. Some servers that run Gemma 4 expect the role tool_responses instead, and answer an error or ignore the result otherwise.

The extension changes the role for such models: when the Model of an inference provider contains gemma4 or gemma-4 (in any letter case), the results of function calls to it are sent as tool_responses. Requests to other models are not touched. It is a port of the SillyTavern extension SillyTavern-Gemma4-Tools-Fix.
There is nothing to configure. Load the extension in Admin → Extensions; it applies to the next request.

Everything you create in LingoLLM belongs to your account: language profiles, inference providers and settings. Other users don't see them (except an inference provider an administrator shares), and you don't see theirs.
The buttons at the bottom of the workspace:

The language of the user interface, see Language.

Changes your password, user name and full name, see below.

Change Password opens a dialog with your Username, Full Name, Current Password, Password and Repeat password:
enter your current password for every change (leave it empty if your account has no password);
to change the password, enter the new one in both password fields;
leave both password fields empty to change only the name and keep the password;
the user name must not be used by another account.
Click OK to save. With a wrong current password nothing is saved.

Changing the password ends all saved logins (Save login), on every device including this one: they have to log in again with the new password. If a device was lost or your password leaked, changing the password logs that device out. Sessions that are open right now (a browser tab still showing the workspace) stay logged in until they log out or their session expires.

The Language selector above the buttons switches the user interface to another language. The choice is saved in your account: the page reloads with the new language, and so does every other page you have open (on another device too), and it is used again the next time you log in. The login screen itself is always in the default language.

The list contains only the languages that are installed. English comes with LingoLLM; an administrator can add more by loading an extension. Texts a language doesn't translate are shown in English. Dates are written the way that language does. This is the language of the interface, not a language you learn (those are your language profiles).
Save login on the login screen keeps you logged in on this device for 30 days (it needs HTTPS on a server, see Server (Docker)). Logout ends it.

An account can have an empty password; you then log in with the user name only. If an administrator cleared your forgotten password, log in this way and set a new password with Change Password right away. That is handy for the desktop app on your own computer, but never do it on a server others can reach.
The Settings tab holds your personal settings.
At the top are two buttons:
Discard Changes - throws away the unsaved changes and loads the saved settings again;
Save - saves the settings.

Settings are not saved automatically. As soon as you change a field (extension settings included), Unsaved changes appears at the top and the other tabs, Admin and Logout are locked. Click Save or Discard Changes to unlock them.

The inference provider that is used when nothing else is chosen.
Settings of the installed extensions, one section per extension. They are saved with the same Save button. The tab is empty when no extension with settings is installed.

Administrators manage the LingoLLM installation: user accounts, database backups, cleanup of deleted data and extensions. The first account, created on the first start, is an administrator; it can make other users administrators too.
Administrators are also normal users with their own language profiles - they don't see other users' profiles or settings.

Administrators have an Admin button at the bottom of the workspace. It is only in the normal layout: the phone layout (a window narrower than 768 pixels) has no Admin page, so open LingoLLM in a wider window (and reload the page) for administration. It opens the admin page with four tabs:
Tab
Users
Creating, editing and deleting accounts. See Users.
Database Backups
Backups of the whole database, on demand or on a schedule, and restoring them. See Database backups.

Permanently removing deleted data. See Cleanup.
Extensions
Installing and removing extensions. See Managing extensions.
Everything LingoLLM stores is in the .lingollm folder in the home directory of the user that runs it (./data on the host with the Docker setup):
Path

The database: users, language profiles, chats, settings, everything.

Key that encrypts the API keys in the database. Created on the first start; without it, saved API keys can't be read.

Database backups.

The files each user uploaded (Resources).
extensions/
Installed extension JARs.

Logs of the desktop app.

To back up a whole installation, stop LingoLLM and copy this folder (including secret.key). While it runs, use database backups for the database; uploaded files and extensions are plain files and can be copied at any time.
The Users tab of the admin page lists all accounts with their Username, Full Name and whether they are an Administrator.
Click Add User.
Fill in Username, Full Name, Password and Repeat password.
Check Administrator if the user should manage the installation.
Click OK.
Give the user name and password to the person; they can change the password later themselves (see Account & settings).

LingoLLM accepts an account with an empty password - anyone can then log in with just the user name. Only do that on the desktop app on your own computer. Creating a user without a password asks for confirmation first.
The user name must be unique.
The pen button opens the same dialog for an existing user:
change the user name, full name and the administrator flag;
leave both password fields empty to keep the user's password as it is;
to set a new password, enter it in both password fields;
to clear the password, tick Clear password (the password fields are disabled) and confirm. The account then has no password.
You don't need the user's current password for any of this. A new or cleared password ends all the user's saved logins.
LingoLLM has no password reset by e-mail. Either:
set a new password here and tell it to the user, who can change it later with Change Password; or

tick Clear password, tell the user to log in with their user name and an empty password, and to set a new password right away with Change Password (leave Current Password empty). The administrator never learns the new password this way.
Until the user sets a new password, anyone who knows the user name can log in to a cleared account. On a server, clear the password only when the user can log in right away.
The last administrator can't lose the administrator flag: The last administrator cannot be deleted or demoted.

By default every user adds their own inference providers. Uncheck Users can create their own models above the user list to stop that: users can then only use the providers the administrators share. The providers a user already has keep working and can still be edited; administrators can always add providers.
The trash button deletes the account after confirming. You can't delete your own account or the last administrator.
The user can no longer log in, saved logins on their devices stop working, and the user name becomes free for a new account.

Their language profiles (with chats and messages), inference providers (with their API keys) and settings disappear with the account - nobody can see them any more - and the next Cleanup removes them from the database together with the account.

The user's files (uploaded images and resources) are kept: their folder in the data directory is renamed to login-deleted (login-deleted-2... if that name is taken), so a new account with the same user name starts with an empty folder. Delete the renamed folder by hand once you don't need it.

A database backup is a complete copy of the LingoLLM database: all users with all their language profiles, chats, settings and extension data. Use it to protect the installation against mistakes and failures, and to move it to another computer.

Click Create Backup on the Database Backups tab. The copy is made while LingoLLM runs, consistent even when people are writing. It appears in the list with its Name, Created date, Type (Manual or Scheduled) and Size. The toolbar shows the current size of the database.
Each backup has:
Button
Download
Downloads the backup file (.sqlite) - keep a copy outside the server.
Restore on restart
Restores the backup, see below.
trash
Deletes the backup.

Upload Backup adds a backup file (.sqlite or .db) to the list, for example one downloaded from another installation. The file is checked first and refused with The database can't be restored: ... and the reason when it is not a SQLite database, is damaged, is not a LingoLLM database (another application's database), or comes from a newer LingoLLM version than the one running.

A database backup contains everything, including the password hashes of all users and their API keys. The API keys are encrypted with the secret.key file in the data folder, which is not part of the backup - but anyone with both the backup and secret.key can read them. Keep downloaded backups as safe as the server itself.

The files are stored in the db-backups folder of the data folder. Copies LingoLLM makes itself - pre-restore-... before a restore and pre-migration-... before an upgrade - are in the list too, shown as Manual, so they are never deleted by the rotation of scheduled backups. Uploaded files and extension JARs are separate files and are not part of a database backup.

Uploaded files are not part of a database backup either. The database only knows them as entries of the Resources tab; the files are in the data/login/images folder of the data folder. That is fine: after a restore the entries are the ones from the time of the backup and the files they use are still in the folder. Files that were added after the backup are just left over (nothing refers to them) and take disk space. To keep the files safe, include the whole data folder in your own backups.

When you restore a backup on another installation, copy secret.key from the original installation as well (with LingoLLM stopped), otherwise the saved API keys can't be decrypted and every user has to enter them again.
The Scheduled Backups section creates backups automatically:
Field

Turns scheduled backups on.
Schedule (cron)
When to create them, see below. The next three times are shown under the field.
Keep scheduled backups
How many scheduled backups to keep; older ones are deleted. 0 keeps all. Manual and uploaded backups are never deleted.
Click Save Schedule to apply it. The status line shows when the last scheduled backup was made and when the next one is due.
When LingoLLM wasn't running at a scheduled time - typical for the desktop app, which runs only while you write - it makes the missed backup about 30 seconds after the next start.
The schedule is a cron expression with five fields, minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week:
Expression
Runs
every day at 3:00
every 6 hours
Mondays at 2:30 (day of week: 0 or 7 is Sunday, 1 Monday...)
on the 1st of every month at noon
@daily, @weekly, @monthly

Times are in the time zone of the server (in Docker, set it with the TZ environment variable).

To turn scheduled backups off, uncheck Create backups automatically and click Save Schedule. The expression is kept, so you can turn the backups on again later. It is still checked - an invalid expression is never saved - but while the backups are off, the field may also be empty.
A database can't be replaced while LingoLLM uses it, so a restore happens on the next start:
Click Restore on restart next to the backup and confirm. The tab shows Database restore is scheduled. Restart the application to apply it. - Cancel Restore undoes it.
Restart LingoLLM: quit and start the desktop app, or docker compose restart on the server.

On the start, the current database is moved to db-backups/pre-restore-time-lingollm.sqlite - it appears in the list, so a restore can be undone by restoring that file - and the backup takes its place. A backup from an older LingoLLM version is upgraded automatically.

The backup is checked again before it is swapped in (the same checks as for Upload Backup, also Restore on restart refuses a backup that fails them). If it fails the check, or upgrading it fails, LingoLLM keeps (or puts back) the current database and starts normally; the refused file is moved to db-backups/rejected-restore-time-lingollm.sqlite and the log says why.
Everything after the backup is lost: profiles, chats and settings created since. Users who are logged in have to log in again if their account changed.

When a new version of LingoLLM is going to change the structure of an existing database, it first saves a copy as db-backups/pre-migration-time-Vversion-lingollm.sqlite, where the version is the one the database was at. The copy is in the list of backups, so an upgrade can be undone by installing the old version of LingoLLM and restoring that copy. The last three copies are kept. A new installation has nothing to copy, and if the copy can't be made (for example the disk is full), the log says so and the upgrade goes on.
A migration that fails halfway is rolled back by itself and LingoLLM does not start; the copy is for an upgrade that went through but did something you don't want.

l: Starting from scratch with a SQL file
p: For setting up a server or a test installation you can make LingoLLM delete all its data and start again from a SQL file (for example one with your users and models). Start it with the VM argument -Dreinitialize-with-sql=/path/to/file.sql (the desktop app: --reinitialize-with-sql /path/to/file.sql). On that start the whole .lingollm folder is emptied - database, backups, resources and extensions; only secret.key, the key that encrypts the API keys, stays -, the database is created, the file is run on it, and LingoLLM starts as usual. Nothing is deleted if the file cannot be read.
To make such a file from an existing installation, dump only the data, with the column names so the file survives a change of the columns (the sqlite3 command line tool, version 3.50 or newer):
A file made by .dump works too: its own BEGIN/COMMIT lines are ignored, because the file is run in one transaction anyway.

Everything is deleted, and it is deleted again at every start that has the argument. Take it out of the command line (or docker-compose.yml) once LingoLLM has started. Encrypted API keys in the file only work if they were encrypted with the secret.key that stays in the folder.

c:
DB=~/.lingollm/lingollm.sqlite
for t in $(sqlite3 "$DB" "SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'table' AND name NOT LIKE 'sqlite_%' AND name <> 'flyway_schema_history'"); do
  sqlite3 "$DB" ".headers on" ".mode insert $t" "SELECT * FROM $t;"
done > init.sql

p: Create a backup and Download it.
Install LingoLLM on the new computer, create a temporary administrator on the first start.
Upload Backup, Restore on restart, restart.
Log in with the accounts from the backup.
Copy the data folder (the uploaded files) and extensions folder from the old data folder as well. Or simply stop LingoLLM and copy the whole .lingollm folder.

When users delete something in LingoLLM - a language profile, a chat, an inference provider - it disappears from their lists, but stays in the database. That makes deleting safe and keeps references working (a chat still knows the provider that answered). Until then users can restore their deleted objects from the Trash tab. Cleanup removes such deleted data for good, to keep the database small.
Cleanup can't be undone, what it removes is gone from the Trash too. Create a database backup first.
Open the Cleanup tab of the admin page and click Analyze. Nothing is changed yet.
Check the result (see below).
Click Run Cleanup and confirm n objects will be permanently removed.
Cleanup covers the data of all users.
Files are not removed. Cleanup deletes entries from the database only; the files of deleted resources (files you uploaded) stay in the data folder of their owner.

Trash below the tables lists the deleted objects of all users, one row per object (open it to load the table), so you can see what a cleanup would remove and restore what somebody asked you to bring back. The Extensions tab of the admin page installs and removes extensions for the whole installation.
Actions
Active when it is running; Stopped when you stopped it (see Stopping and starting); Installed or Resolved when it failed to start (see When an extension fails).

Click Load Extension (.jar) (or drop the file on it) and choose the extension's JAR file. It is copied to the extensions folder of the data folder and started right away; Extension loaded successfully. confirms it. The extension appears in the list:
Column
Extension Name

Extensions change parts of the user interface of one LingoLLM version. Use the extensions built from the same source as the application (see the plugins README). An incompatible extension may fail to load or break parts of the application. The extension API is not frozen in 1.0, so expect to update extensions together with LingoLLM.
ID
Its name.
Its version. The # button next to it shows the SHA-256 hash of the extension's JAR when you hover it; click it to copy the hash, e.g. to compare it with the one published by the author.

JAR files can also be copied into the extensions folder directly, for example on a server without access to the UI; they are loaded on the next start. This is also how the Docker setup can be prepared: put the JARs into ./data/extensions. The JARs can be built in Docker too, see Plugins in the server guide.
State
Stop / Start, Log and Unload.
The internal number of the extension in this run.
Users see the extension in windows they open from then on - the page has to be reloaded.
Valid or Invalid; click it to read the report of the check LingoLLM made before starting the extension.
Verification
Version

Stop unloads the extension immediately without removing it: it disappears from the screens it added to, but its JAR and data stay, and it is listed with the state Stopped. The button then reads Start, which loads it again (it is checked first, like at the start of the application; if the check fails, it stays stopped and the report is shown). A stopped extension stays stopped after LingoLLM restarts. Uploading a new version of a stopped extension starts it.

The stop is remembered by an empty file named like the JAR with .STOPPED added (sidequery.jar.STOPPED) in the extensions folder. On a server without access to the UI, create it to keep an extension from starting, or delete it to let the extension start on the next start.

Log opens the log of the extension: what the extension itself wrote with the logger LingoLLM gives to extensions (Logging). It shows the last part of the file, Refresh reads it again and Clear deletes it. The file is extensions/name.jar.log (for example sidequery.jar.log); when it grows over 2 MB it is moved to .log.old and a new one is started. It is deleted when the extension is unloaded. Extensions that don't log anything have an empty log. What the extension logs also goes to the application log (named extension.name, at the level of the line), so it is in the log of the server too; problems of LingoLLM itself are only there.

Unload asks for confirmation, then stops the extension immediately and deletes its JAR (and its log) from the extensions folder. Its data stays (see Where extension data is kept); loading it again brings the data back.

To install a newer version of an extension, Load Extension (.jar) with the new file - the file name doesn't matter. The installed version is unloaded, its JAR deleted and the new version started in its place. If the new version fails to load, the upload shows the error and the old version keeps running.
If an uploaded extension can't be loaded, the upload shows Failed to load extension: ... and its JAR is not kept.

LingoLLM checks an extension against the version it is running in before it starts it. An extension that does not fit - typically one built for another version of LingoLLM - is not loaded. An upload shows the report of the check and is not kept; an extension in the extensions folder stays in the list, not started, with Invalid in the Verification column, and the report is in the log. The check is repeated after LingoLLM is updated, so an extension that worked before can be refused afterwards: get the version of the extension that was built for the new version of LingoLLM and load it. Next to each extension's JAR you'll find a small .valid or .invalid file with the report; it is removed with the extension and can be left alone.

An extension in the extensions folder that fails to start (for example one built for another version) doesn't stop the others from loading. It is listed with the state Installed or Resolved instead of Active and can be removed with Unload. A file that isn't an extension at all is skipped and not listed - delete it from the extensions folder. The log (docker compose logs, or desktop/logs/lingollm.log for the desktop app) has the details of the error.
Most problems leave a trace in the log:
Installation
Log
Desktop app
~/.lingollm/desktop/logs/lingollm.log (%USERPROFILE%\.lingollm\desktop\logs on Windows); the previous run is in lingollm.log.1
Docker
docker compose logs -f lingollm
Error dialogs in the application (Internal Server Error) show the error as well; the log has the full details.
macOS says the app "is damaged" or "can't be opened". The app isn't signed yet. Right-click it and choose Open, or run xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/LingoLLM.app. See Desktop app.

Which model should I use? Any model that is good in the language you learn and has a large enough context; a context of 32 000 tokens or more is comfortable.

p: Vaadin runs either in development mode (frontend served from a development bundle that Vaadin builds into src/main/bundles/, ignored by Git; Vaadin's dev tools available, more checks) or in production mode (optimized frontend bundle, no dev tools). The mode is decided by META-INF/VAADIN/config/flow-build-info.json, the build info that vaadin-maven-plugin writes:
prepare-frontend (every build, also mvn compile and mvn jetty:run) writes a development build info with the absolute paths of your checkout into target/classes;
build-frontend (in prepare-package, so only mvn package / install) builds the optimized bundle, writes a production build info into the WAR and removes the development one from target/classes.

By default Vaadin scans the bytecode of the app and puts only the components it finds referenced into the production bundle. Extensions are loaded at runtime and may use any Vaadin component, so the plugin is configured with optimizeBundlefalse/optimizeBundle (-Dvaadin.devmode.optimizeBundle=false on the command line): the bundle contains every component on the classpath, at the price of a bigger bundle and a slower frontend build.

So mvn package always produces a production WAR - the one the Dockerfile, the desktop profile and CI use, and the one to deploy. Nothing has to be copied around. A build info in src/main/resources is never packaged into the WAR (maven-war-plugin excludes META-INF/VAADIN/config/flow-build-info.json*).

Development mode is for running from the IDE (see IntelliJ IDEA) or mvn jetty:run. Without a build info Vaadin also starts in development mode and finds the project by the vaadin.project.basedir system property, the classpath or the working directory.
To check a WAR:

c: unzip -p target/lingollm-1.2.0.war WEB-INF/classes/META-INF/VAADIN/config/flow-build-info.json   # "productionMode" : true

p: LingoLLM relies on compile-time AspectJ weaving with the spring-aspects library: Vaadin components are created with new, not by Spring, so classes annotated @Configurable (all routes, the workspace, dialogs, parts...) get their @Autowired fields injected by the woven AnnotationBeanConfigurerAspect.
Transactions are not woven: @CommonTx, @CommonTxReadOnly and @NoTx are applied by Spring's class-based proxies around the service beans (see Services).

If the classes are compiled by plain javac, nothing fails at build time, but at runtime every @Autowired field of a UI class is null and the first screen fails with a NullPointerException. Maven always uses ajc; in your IDE, make sure the AspectJ compiler is used too (see IntelliJ IDEA).

The compiler also keeps parameter names (-parameters) and all local variables (preserveAllLocals): extensions read method arguments and local variables of @Extendable methods by name, so don't remove these options.
LingoLLM is a plain WAR without an embedded server, so you run it in a servlet container: from the IDE, with mvn jetty:run, in a local Jetty, or in Docker.

LingoLLM is one Java web application running in one JVM. There is no separate frontend project, no REST API and no external database: the browser shows Vaadin components that live on the server, the components call Spring services, and the services store everything in a single SQLite file. Calls to an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API run on background threads and push their results to the browser. Extensions are OSGi bundles loaded into the same JVM; they change the UI by hooking into methods of instrumented classes.

Server-side UI. Vaadin Flow keeps the component tree on the server; the browser renders it and sends events back. UI code is ordinary Java that calls services directly - there is no API layer to keep in sync.

Spring without Spring Boot. The application context is built from XML files; services and repositories are explicit beans. Vaadin components are created with new and get their dependencies through AspectJ-woven @Configurable.
One file of data. SQLite in WAL mode, schema managed by Flyway, mapped by Hibernate. Backing up an installation means copying one folder.
Multi-user, single process. Every entity belongs to a user; services filter by the user of the current HTTP session. All users share one JVM and one database.
Language profiles. A user has several language profiles; everything learned belongs to one, and the profile of the session is a session-scoped bean (Domain model).
Runtime extensions. OSGi bundles can be loaded and unloaded without a restart. The UI classes they extend are instrumented at startup so that any of their methods can be decorated.

The container finds Spring's SpringServletContainerInitializer, which calls ui/main/WebappApplicationInitializer. It creates an XmlWebApplicationContext from META-INF/spring/application-config.xml and registers the ContextLoaderListener, the RequestContextListener (makes request and session scoped beans work) and the SessionTrackingListener (feeds HTTP sessions to the SessionManager, see Sessions).

Configuration resolves the data folder (user.home/.lingollm) and creates its subfolders. When the data source asks for the database URL (configuration.resolveDb(...)), a staged database restore (lingollm.sqlite.restore) is swapped in first - a restore can't replace a database that is open. Then a copy of an existing database that is behind the bundled migrations is saved in db-backups (pre-migration-*, see Startup).

Vaadin UI state may only be changed while holding the session lock. Code on other threads - backups, long running requests - updates the UI with ui.access(...), and the change reaches the browser through server push (@Push on AppShellConfig, WebSocket with long-polling fallback). Two helpers make this safe:
UIPushGuard.push(ui) pushes explicitly but never re-entrantly from the same thread.

Background threads have no HTTP request, so session-scoped beans (the current user and language) would not resolve. Code that starts background work captures the request attributes in a ThreadCopyRequestAttributes and wraps the work in ThreadCopyRequestAttributes.InRequestScope, which makes the session of the user who started it current on the worker thread.
bound/SessionManager (bean sessionManager, defined in container-config.xml) knows every HTTP session of the application and which user is logged into it.

Tracking. SessionTrackingListener is an HttpSessionListener registered in WebappApplicationInitializer; it looks the bean up in the root context and calls onSessionCreate / onSessionDestroy. Each session gets a SessionInformation. After a successful login Main calls userLoggedIn(user, VaadinSession), which fills it in once: the Vaadin session, the user, the current UI as the main UI and a ThreadCopyRequestAttributes copy of the request. Note that login calls VaadinService.reinitializeSession - the old session is destroyed and a new one created, so the bound session is the new one.

Running code in other sessions. runForUsers(test, runnable, uiBound) runs a RunInSession for every session whose user matches the predicate, with that session's request attributes in scope (so the session-scoped user resolves to that user). With uiBound the runnable is queued with VaadinSession.access on a live UI of the session (the main UI, or any other open one if it was closed) - it runs asynchronously, once the session lock is free, and changes are pushed when the lock is released. The sessions are processed on a separate thread (ThreadUtils.executeInThread), so the caller's Vaadin and request thread locals don't leak into them; the call waits for the dispatch, not for the queued access tasks. The skipCurrent overload leaves out the caller's own Vaadin session. UserServiceImpl.changePassword / clearPassword use it to invalidate the other sessions of the user whose password changed - a user changing their own password stays logged in in the current session.

Open UIs. After login Main registers their UI in ApplicationPoint (bean applicationPoint) with the workspace and a copy of the user. SessionInformation.getUI(workspaceClass, applicationPoint) / getWorkspace(...) find the session's UI showing a given workspace type.

Dead UI detection. SessionManager is also a daemon thread (Inactive session watcher), started by afterPropertiesSet and stopped on context shutdown. Every DEAD_SESSION_CHECK_TIMEOUT / 10 seconds (see Constants) it tryLocks each logged-in session - a locked session is in use and skipped - and closes UIs whose last heartbeat is older than the timeout. Threads queued on the session lock count as activity. The timeout is never shorter than three Vaadin heartbeat intervals (5 minutes by default), otherwise an open but idle tab would be closed between two heartbeats. When every UI of the session is closing, the HTTP session is invalidated.

Close notifications. addSessionCloseListener registers a SessionCloseListener on the current session. When another session is destroyed, every listener of every remaining session is called inside its own session's access and request scope with the SessionInformation of the closed session.
getActiveUsers(), getOpenedSessions(user), getSessionInformation(id) and getActiveSessionIds() expose the registry, e.g. for admin views.

Loading. Extensions are OSGi bundles run by an embedded Apache Felix framework (OsgiServiceImpl). Boot delegation is open for all packages (org.osgi.framework.bootdelegation=*, parent = the framework's class loader, which is the web application's), so bundles see the application's classes and libraries directly without importing them. A bundle registers a LingoLLMExtension service; LingoLLM calls onExtensionLoad / onExtensionUnload and passes the ExtensionService. Before an extension is started, ExtensionService.verifyExtension checks the classes, methods, arguments, locals and fields its decorators use against the running application (the result is kept in name.valid / name.invalid next to the JAR); an extension that doesn't fit is not started.

Instrumentation. At startup a ByteBuddy agent rewrites every non-static, non-constructor method of each class annotated @Extendable: ExtendableMethodVisitor adds a call to ExtensionService.onExtendableMethodEnter at the start, records each local variable as it is stored, and calls onExtendableMethodLeave on every return and throw (at the return of a value the original value is registered first and the one the decorators leave is returned). This happens on every call, with or without decorators, so @Extendable belongs on UI classes, not on hot code.

Decorators. ExtensionService.registerDecorator(decorator, className, methodName) attaches code before and after a method. Through the ExtendableMethodContext it can read the method's arguments, read local variables by name (for example the menu the method just built, to add an item to it) and access fields and methods reflectively. On enter it can replace arguments, on leave it can replace the return value (chained through the decorators); it can't skip the method.

Data. Extensions keep their data in the attributes of existing entities, so no schema changes are needed and the data is part of backups. They can also take part in cleanup (CleanupService.registerContributor).

UI lifetime. An extension registers the components it adds with OsgiService.bindAttachableComponent together with a callback that removes them; the callbacks of components still attached run when the extension is unloaded, each inside ui.access(...) of the component's UI.

Languages. An extension that implements ExtensionHasLocalization adds languages to the UI: OsgiServiceImpl registers its LocalizationBundles in Localization after the extension loads and removes them on unload (Localization).

Styles. An extension that implements ExtensionHasCss gets its CSS put into every open page: CssRegistry (owned by Main) reads the loaded extensions when its page is attached and listens to the loaded/unloaded events of OsgiService afterwards (Styles of a plugin).
Because hooks are attached by class and method name and read local variables by name, extensions are tied to one version of the application. See Plugin development.

All UI texts are looked up through the Localization bean by an L key (loc.getValue(L.LABEL_SAVE)). The bean (LocalizationImpl) holds one LocalizationBundle per Language: the texts of every key, the Locale and the date formats of that language, and the name shown in the language selector. The application ships LocalizationBundleEN (the default language, which has to be complete - the application doesn't start otherwise), listed in the localization bean in container-config.xml. The English bundle holds only the keys the code uses (a stub): other languages come with extensions or are added later.

Which language. getValue and the formats use the language in the session's SessionPoint. Without a request (startup, scheduled backups) or with a language that has no bundle (any more) the default language is used, and a text a bundle doesn't have is taken from the default language, so a bundle that lags behind the keys keeps working. Worker threads get the session through ThreadCopyRequestAttributes like the user bean. The names of the learnable languages (Languages) are ENUM_LANGUAGE_* keys, see Localization.getLanguageName; the CEFR levels (CEFR) are ENUM_CEFR_* keys, see Localization.getCefrLevel.

Choosing. The language of a user is UserSetting.language (a language code, null for the default). Main.proceedWithLogin sets SessionPoint.language from it before the workspace is created, so the login page itself is always in the default language. The LanguageSelector at the bottom of the workspace (desktop sidebar, phone drawer) offers Localization.getAvailableLanguages(); a change saves the setting, sets the session and reloads every UI of every session of the user (SessionManager.runForUsers), where the workspace opens again with the new language.

Extensions. An extension that implements ExtensionHasLocalization returns bundles of its own; OsgiServiceImpl registers them after onExtensionLoad and removes them when the extension is unloaded (see the example plugin shows the extension class). A language that already has a bundle is refused, so an extension can't replace English.

Adding a language to the application. Copy LocalizationBundleEN, translate, add the class as a bean to the bundles list of localization. A bundle other than the default one may miss keys (they fall back to English); the default one must have every key of L, LocalizationImpl refuses to start otherwise.

Most of an entity's data is not in table columns but in one JSON document stored in the extendedContent blob. Two kinds of fields end up there:
fields annotated @ExtendedAttribute (they are also @Transient, so Hibernate ignores them), and

attributes, a free-form JsonObject for extensions. Its keys are stored with the prefix attributes_ next to the other fields. Any JsonObject field can be stored this way (so can a POJO, see Types) with @ExtendedAttribute(inject = true, injectPrefix = name); Language.languageSpecificData does (keys languageSpecificData_*), attributes is the same mechanism.
ExtendableEntityListener converts between the fields and the document:

Load (@PostLoad): the JSON is parsed and the fields are set. Supported field types are String, numbers, Boolean, Date (ISO-8601 instant in UTC, e.g. 2026-10-09T08:15:30.123Z; values in the old yyyy.MM.dd'Z'HH:mm:ss.SSS format, written in the server's time zone, are still read), enums (by name) and for inject = true a JsonObject or any class Gson can read (below).

Injected POJOs: an inject = true field may also be a class (or a list, map...): it is converted with Gson; an object is flattened by its top-level properties (prefix_name), nested parts stay structured, and a value that is not an object (a list) is stored under the plain prefix. A field absent from the content keeps its default value.

Types: the values are written with toString(), so a field can't be a collection. A list is kept as a JSON string in a String field with typed accessors, like FreeChatMessage.attachments (getAttachments() / setAttachments(...), a JSON array of ImageAttachment(resource uuid, caption)).
Save: JpaExtendableRepository.save serializes the fields into extendedContent before the entity is written.

Because the fields are @Transient, Hibernate's dirty checking doesn't see them. A change to an extended attribute is only stored by calling the service's save. Changing it on a managed entity and letting the transaction commit does nothing.

saveWithoutEvent writes extendedContent as it is, without serializing the fields first. It is used when extendedContent was set directly - copying the JSON of a backup into a restored entity - and must not be overwritten by the (empty) fields. The repository then reads the fields back from the JSON and rebuilds _fulltext from them.

l: Limits of the users of a shared AI
p: AI.limits is an @ExtendedAttribute string holding a JSON object: the AILimit of each user under the user's uuid (strategy LimitStrategy UNLIMITED / TOKEN_LIMIT / NOT_AVAILABLE, resetStrategy ResetStrategy DAILY / WEEKLY / MONTHLY, and prefillTokens, generatedTokens, totalTokens, each null for unlimited). AILimits reads and writes it; a user without an entry is not limited. These are only the settings and they are set by the owner (an administrator). What a user used is not in this JSON on purpose: it changes with every request, from the thread of any user, and AIService.save is for the owner and would lose parallel updates, so it is in the two period* columns of the user's Usage, added up in SQL like the other counters.

The reset is lazy. ResetStrategy.periodStart(now) is the start of the calendar day / week (from Monday) / month in the server's time zone. UsageService.add (under record) of a user with a TOKEN_LIMIT first runs UsageRepository.resetPeriod (zeroes the period counters when lastUsed is before the period start) and then adds; for a user without one it zeroes them. AILimitService.getStatus does not write: it reports 0 used when lastUsed is before the period start. LimitStatus.block(promptTokens) is the first reached of the sent, generated and total limits, or NOT_AVAILABLE. The prompt is known before the request, so a request is refused when the sent (or total) counter is at its limit or the estimated prompt (approximatePromptTokens, our count) would take it over; the generated counter is only compared with its limit, so the last response can go over - unless AILimit.hardGeneratedLimit is set: then the generated counter plus the response the request reserves (the AI's maxCompletionTokens; 0 when there is none) has to fit into the generated limit. The hard flag does not apply to the total limit. AILimit.validate() rejects negative numbers and, when all three are set, sent plus generated below the total (the total could never be reached).

The same reference model drives the trash (TrashService, implemented by CleanupServiceImpl; Trash tab and Admin → Cleanup). It lists the soft-deleted rows of every root entity that is an OwnedEntity (AI stands for its subclasses) with narrow projections - the extendedContent blob is only read by getExtendedContent, which pretty-prints it - and restores them with a bulk UPDATE ... SET deleted = false, modification = now, so no entity listener runs and extended attributes stay untouched. Before it restores, it looks up the parents of the selected rows:

When a parent is deleted and not part of the same selection, nothing is restored and the result lists the blockers. A deleted owner counts as a parent, so the objects of a deleted user can't be restored.

The restore is the reverse of the soft delete cascade: the selection is first extended with the deleted rows it owns (OWNED_BY rows pointing at a selected row, rows a selected row OWNS, repeatedly), so restoring a language profile brings back its chats and messages, and RestoreResult.getRestored() counts them too. It can't tell a row that was deleted together with its owner from one deleted on its own earlier, so the latter comes back as well. A restored message whose children were moved to its parent (a permanent delete) does not get them back.

TrashService.deletePermanently removes deleted rows for good, for the Delete Permanently button of TrashGrid. It is limited to getPermanentlyDeletableTypes() (FreeChatMessage; anything else raises IllegalArgumentException) so a user can't purge a whole profile, and checks ownership like restore. It runs the purge of the cleanup (executePurge) on the selection; a block by a CleanupContributor (or any other row that would have to go) makes the whole call return DeleteResult.getBlocked() and roll back. Before that, moveChildrenOfMessages moves the children of the selected messages - deleted ones too - to the nearest ancestor that is not selected, with bulk updates, so removing a chain of messages keeps the messages below it connected.
So a deleted provider that something still uses shows up as blocked on the Cleanup page, while a deleted language profile takes its chats and messages with it.

Because the soft delete deletes the owned rows too, they are purge roots of their own. A root whose owner (OWNED_BY, directly or through other rows) is blocked is held back: it stays, is not listed as blocked itself and is not counted as purgeable, so a blocked chat that is still restorable keeps its messages.

Before the data source is created, Configuration.resolveDb swaps in a staged database restore, if there is one (see Database backups and restores). Then Configuration.backupBeforeMigration asks DatabaseCheck.pendingMigrationFrom whether the existing file is behind the newest bundled Vn migration (or has no history table, which Flyway baselines at V1). If so it saves a VACUUM INTO copy as db-backups/pre-migration-time-Vfrom-lingollm.sqlite and keeps the newest three. A new installation (no file or an empty one) and a current database are left alone, and a copy that fails is logged, not fatal. The check looks at the Flyway history only, so a Java Migration bean without a Vn file does not trigger a copy.
Cause

Flyway runs every pending migration from classpath:migration (src/main/resources/migration/) and records it in flyway_schema_history. baselineOnMigrate=true with baseline version 1 makes databases created before Flyway was introduced (V1 schema without a history table) start at V1 and get V2 onwards.
Hibernate builds the EntityManagerFactory and validates the schema against the entities: every mapped table and column must exist with a compatible type. It never creates or alters anything.
If either step fails, the Spring context doesn't start and LingoLLM doesn't serve any page; the cause is in the log. Typical messages:
Message
Migration Vn__... failed
No data migration exists yet (the list in applicationInitializer is empty and appVersion is 1).

Reinitialization, a development aid for the time before 1.0.0, when V1__initial.sql is edited instead of adding migrations: after changing V1, start with a SQL file that reloads your test data (only with the VM argument -Dreinitialize-with-sql=/path/to/file.sql, or the desktop launcher option --reinitialize-with-sql file): Configuration.afterPropertiesSet reads the script into memory, then wipes the content of the application folder (~/.lingollm) before anything is created in it. The folder itself, secret.key (so encrypted values in the script stay readable) and the launcher's own desktop/ subfolder (the Jetty base of the running desktop app) stay. Nothing is deleted when the script is not a readable file or the folder is a filesystem root or the home folder. Then resolveDb has Flyway create and migrate the database (the Flyway of step 2 has nothing left to do) and runs the script on it in one transaction (lines with only BEGIN, COMMIT or END are dropped first, so a sqlite3 .dump can be used; Spring ScriptUtils: statements end with ;, so a trigger body with ; inside does not work). A script that fails is rolled back and stops the startup. The argument wipes the data at every start it is present for, so it has to be removed after the start.

Names. Tables are plural (languages, free_chats, free_chat_messages), set by @Table(name = ...). Columns use the Java field name (nameOverride, maxContext); relations end in _id (language_id, parentChat_id), except the owner, which is userId, and the soft delete flag, is_deleted. No foreign key constraints. The tables have no REFERENCES clauses (SQLite wouldn't enforce them: PRAGMA foreign_keys is off). Integrity is kept by the application: rows are soft deleted, so references stay valid, and the admin Cleanup follows the cleanup references to decide what may be purged. Code that hard deletes must clear or move references itself (see CleanupServiceImpl.moveChildrenOfMessages). Because cleanup nulls references before it purges, a column that holds one must be nullable in the table (free_chat_messages.parentChat_id, usages.ai_id).

Enums. AI.aiType is stored as an ordinal (tinyint), all other enums by name. SaneSQLiteDialect turns off the CHECK constraints that Hibernate would otherwise generate for enum columns, so a new enum value doesn't need a table rebuild.
Large values. Text that can be long (name, uri, apiKey...) is @Lob → clob; extendedContent is a blob with JSON. SQLite doesn't enforce lengths, so varchar(255) is only documentation.
Encrypted columns. Secrets are stored encrypted, see Encrypted columns.

OpenAICompatible.apiKey is mapped with @Convert(converter = EncryptedStringConverter.class). The converter calls Configuration.encrypt / decrypt:

On the first start Configuration writes a random UUID to data folder/secret.key; the AES-256 key is the SHA-256 of that UUID. The file is outside the database, so a database backup alone doesn't reveal the secrets.

A stored value is enc: + Base64 of a random 12-byte IV and the AES/GCM ciphertext. A function is a method of an interface that is asynchronous - its first parameter is a FunctionContinuationR that the implementation completes (from any thread) with the result or fails - and annotated @LLMFunction, its other parameters @LLMParam:

FunctionRegistry compiles an interface once (FunctionCompiler: JSON schema of the parameters, validation of the method shape) and bind makes a FunctionSet of an implementation. When the model ends its answer with calls, the service runs them as a chain (each on a thread of its own, the first answer of a call wins), appends the calls and their results to its copy of the payload (the list passed in is not changed), asks the model again and goes on until it answers without a call, at most MAX_FUNCTION_ROUNDS times; in the last round the model is told not to call anything. A failed or refused call is reported to the model as an error text. The callback gets one continuous stream (or one result) and onFunctionCall(call, result, failed) for each call. A service that can not call functions throws UnsupportedOperationException.

p: LingoLLM's UI is written in Java with Vaadin Flow 25: the component tree lives on the server, the browser renders it with Vaadin's web components (Lumo theme, dark color scheme) and sends events back over HTTP and a push WebSocket. There is no hand-written frontend code apart from one CSS file. This page explains how the UI code is organized and the conventions to follow when you change it. The code is in ui/.

LingoLLMServlet is the VaadinServlet mapped to /* (with asyncSupported for push).
There is one route, / → Main, which extends LoginCheckRoute.
LoginCheckRoute runs in the route's constructor (showLogin()):
On an empty installation it opens UserDialog in first time mode (create the administrator) and reloads.

Otherwise it tries a user that is already logged in this session (authenticatedSessionUser, overridden by Main: the page was reloaded, e.g. by the language selector) and then the Save login cookies (authenticateFromCookie, rotating the secret on success).

Otherwise it shows a LoginOverlay (PermissiveLoginOverlay - allows empty passwords to reach the server-side check) with the Save login checkbox. The check passes the client address (LoginCheckRoute.clientAddress()) to UserService.authenticate, which throttles failed logins per address (see Login throttling).

After a successful login it calls VaadinService.reinitializeSession (new session id) and the subclass's proceedWithLogin(login), which fills the session-scoped user bean, registers the login with SessionManager.userLoggedIn (see Sessions), sets the language of the session from the user's settings (Localization) and builds the content.
Logout deletes the cookies, closes the Vaadin session, invalidates the HTTP session and redirects to the context root. Cookie names include the context path and the route class.
Most UI classes are not Vaadin components themselves. They are plain classes with a create() method that builds and returns the component tree, and keep references to the fields they need later:
This shape is deliberate:
@Configurable - the class is created with new, and the AspectJ-woven configurer injects its @Autowired fields (services, Localization, the session User and Language). See AspectJ weaving.

@Extendable - the class is instrumented at startup so extensions can run code before and after any of its methods and read its local variables (see Extensions). Small methods with descriptive local variable names (menu, toolbar, headerLayout) are what make a class easy to extend.
Dialogs (AIDialog, UserDialog, LanguageCreationDialog...) extend Vaadin's Dialog but follow the same pattern: construct, call create(), then open().

Workspace is the interface of the top-level layout shown after login (create, refresh, setNavigationLocked, isNavigationLocked, getOnLogout, setOnLogout). Main, the parts, ApplicationPoint and SessionInformation only depend on this interface. DesktopWorkspace is the implementation (@Configurable, @Extendable): it builds an HTabSheet (tabs on the left, a footer with Admin, the language selector, Change Password, Logout) and creates all tab components up front. Each tab is a WorkspaceComponent:

To reload data (after login, after changes elsewhere).

When the tab becomes active - parts reload their lists here.

Workspace.setNavigationLocked(true) disables the other tabs and the Admin and Logout buttons, so the user can't leave the active tab. UserPart locks it while the settings have unsaved changes: it listens to every HasValue in its layout (extension settings panels included) and unlocks on Save, Discard Changes or refresh().

Main.proceedWithLogin picks PhoneWorkspace instead when the body of the page is narrower than 768 px (ExtendedClientDetails.getBodyClientWidth()). The choice is made once per login: resizing or rotating the device does not switch the workspace until the page is reloaded. PhoneWorkspace replaces the left-hand tab sheet with an AppLayout: the parts are listed in a drawer whose footer holds the language selector, Change Password and Logout, and the active part fills the screen. There is no Admin button and no AdminPart on a phone; the services still check AdminGuard.requireAdmin() themselves. The user manual describes this in Using LingoLLM on a phone. PhoneAIPart, PhoneTrashPart and PhoneSettingsPart are phone specific; LanguagePart and ResourcesPart are shared.

l: The Learning tab and the language profiles
p: LanguagePart is the first tab. Its header is a ComboBoxLanguage of the user's profiles (rendered by LanguageItem: flag, name, note) and a + button that opens LanguageCreationDialog. Below it is the component of the LanguageUI that the template of the selected profile creates, Languages.create(workspace).

refresh() loads the profiles, selects the open one, or the one in UserSetting.lastLanguage, or the first; with no profile it clears the session language and opens LanguageCreationDialog with setFirstTime(true) once - the dialog has no cancel button and does not close on Esc or a click outside (the initial setup).

selectLanguage(language, remember) is the one place a profile is chosen. It fills the session-scoped language bean (selectSessionLanguage), optionally saves UserSetting.lastLanguage, and creates the LanguageUI if the profile changed (onTabClosed of the previous one first).
Every selection change goes through the session bean, so services of language bound entities (LanguageBoundServiceImpl.save) put what the user creates into the selected profile.

A LanguageUI (getIcon, getLanguage, setLanguage, plus the WorkspaceComponent methods) is the screen set of one language. LanguageUIBase supplies the plumbing and an empty create(); Japanese and German extend it and are the place to add exercises. To add a language: a constant in Languages (flag from LanguageIcons, defaults from LanguageDefaults, the LanguageUI constructor), its ENUM_LANGUAGE_* key in L, LocalizationBundleEN and LocalizationImpl.loadMaps.

Lists of entities use Vaadin Grid with a lazy data provider. BackendTableProviderBase (in ui.widgets) is the common base: the owning part searches for the ids to show, passes them with setIds(ids), and the provider loads only the entities of the visible page (service.find(id)) and wraps them in a BackendTableItem subclass. It also tracks checked rows. ResourcesPart is a lazy grid over ResourceService.findPageForUser.
