TrashGrid is a self-contained widget (@Configurable, create it with new TrashGrid(allUsers).create()) over TrashService: a lazy multi-select GridTrashItem (items identified by their EntityKey, so the selection survives paging), a filter by type (names from Localization.localizeDomainObject(Class)) and, with allUsers, a filter by owner and an owner column. allUsers only decides what the widget shows; the service decides what the current user may see and restore. Restore Selected confirms and calls TrashService.restore; when it returns blockers the widget shows them in a dialog (nothing was restored), otherwise it refreshes and runs the listeners from addRestoreListener (TrashPart uses it to refresh the whole workspace). Delete Permanently is enabled while the selection has only types of TrashService.getPermanentlyDeletableTypes() (chat messages), confirms and calls TrashService.deletePermanently, shows the reasons in a dialog when it is blocked and refreshes the table otherwise. The Extended Content link opens the JSON from TrashService.getExtendedContent in a read-only text area. TrashPart (the Trash tab, allUsers for administrators) and CleanupPanel (a Details section, created when first opened) both use it.

PhoneTrashGrid (used by PhoneTrashPart) subclasses it through the createToolbar() and addColumns() hooks: the filters are stacked over the whole width, the description is behind an info button, and the table has one content column.

Generic dialogs: ConfirmDialog.show(message, onYes), TextInputDialog.Builder, ListSelectDialog, ErrorDialog (message and expandable stack trace). ExtensionLogDialog.show(bundle, name) is the read-only, monospace view of an extension's log. UsageDialog.show() is the read-only table of every user's Usage (administrators). AILimitsDialog.show(ai) is the table of the limits of a shared AI with add / edit (AILimitEditDialog) / delete, AILimitInfoDialog.show(ai) the current user's limit and usage of it.

Never hard-code user-visible text. Add a key to loc/L.java and the text to LocalizationBundleEN (and to any other bundle), and use loc.getValue(L.KEY) (Localization is injected into every UI class). Date formats come from the same bean (loc.getDateFormat()...). The name of a kind of entity (language profile, chat...) is loc.localizeDomainObject(entityClass); it falls back to the closest known superclass, then to the simple class name, so a new entity type needs a mapping in LocalizationImpl.loadMaps(). The texts are in the language of the user's session, so never keep a text in a field that outlives the page or the request - look it up when you show it (Localization).

Wrap event handlers in try/catch and report unexpected exceptions with UIUtils.internalServerError(loc, e) - it logs the exception and opens an ErrorDialog with the stack trace. Expected problems (validation, missing configuration) are shown with Notification.error(...) or a message next to the field; UIUtils.showValidationErrors(loc, e) formats a binder's ValidationException. Failures of a request to the model API (InferenceException: wrong key, wrong URL, timeout...) go through UIUtils.inferenceError(loc, e), which shows the localized cause (InferenceErrors) as a notification and falls back to internalServerError for anything else. AIDialog has the Test Connection button (InferenceService.testConnection() with the values of the form) and, for administrators only, the Shared with all users checkbox. AIPart / PhoneAIPart list the user's AIs and the shared ones with the user's own Usage (tokens sent / generated); the edit and delete buttons are only shown for AIs the user owns (AIService.isOwnedByCurrentUser) and the add button only when AIService.canCreate(). The service refuses the same things itself. Rows of shared AIs have an info button (AILimitInfoDialog), and the owning administrator a Limits button (AILimitsDialog, AILimitService). AIPart also has a Usage per user button, visible to administrators only, that opens UsageDialog; the service checks the administrator itself.

Forms either save automatically (value change listeners call an autosave() method of the part, guarded so that loading values into the fields doesn't trigger a save) or have an explicit Save, as the Settings tab does. LanguageCreationDialog saves on OK. Entities held by the UI are detached copies - reload them through the service before changing them, and keep the object returned by save.
Vaadin component state may only be touched on a thread holding the session lock. The rules:
Long work (requests to a model, backups, imports) runs on another thread; the UI thread returns immediately.
Updates from that thread go through ui.access(() - ...), with the UI captured on the UI thread (UI.getCurrent() is null elsewhere). UIPushGuard.push(ui) sends them right away.
Service calls on that thread need the user's request scope - capture ThreadCopyRequestAttributes.create() on the UI thread and wrap the work in InRequestScope (see The current user).

Prefer Java components. When the browser has to do something (scroll positions, element sizes), the script is a static method of ui.JavascriptLibrary - UI classes don't call executeJs themselves. The element is passed explicitly ($0, not this), and a script that returns a value returns the PendingJavaScriptResult, read with .then(...); see UIUtils.getPositionAndSizeOfElement and JavascriptLibrary.scrollTextAreaToBottom (the extension log is shown scrolled to its newest line). Extensions keep their own scripts. There are no JavaScript modules of the application.

Global styles are in src/main/frontend/styles/shared-styles.css (imported by AppShellConfig): the loading indicator, Markdown wrapping, the language flags and the utility classes (.text-secondary, .hint-text, .min-width-0...). Each class has a constant in CssStyles with the same name; apply it with addClassName(CssStyles.X) and don't use inline styles (getStyle().set(...)) except for a value computed at runtime. Use Lumo variables (var(--lumo-...)) in the rules. Reuse a class before adding one.

Styles of plugins are not in the stylesheet. Main (the ApplicationEntryPoint) owns a CssRegistry that puts the CSS of extensions implementing ExtensionHasCss into the page and removes it again when the extension is unloaded.

A LingoLLM plugin (the user interface calls them extensions) is an OSGi bundle - a JAR with a few extra manifest headers - that LingoLLM loads at runtime, without a restart. A plugin can add menu items, tabs, panels and settings to the user interface, keep its own data on language profiles, chats and user settings, and add languages of the interface.
This part of the developer guide explains how plugins work and how to write one. It assumes you can build LingoLLM from source (Building from source) and know a little Vaadin Flow (User interface).

One plugin comes with LingoLLM, lingollm/plugins/gemma4toolsfix, the smallest example (a tool role resolver). The mechanism is the one of Marginalia, which has eleven plugins; their code is a good source of patterns, but they hook into Marginalia's classes.
@Extendable hooks
A JSON object on every data entity where a plugin keeps its data - saved with the entity, included in backups, no schema change.
Bundles
Code that runs before and after any method of an instrumented UI class, with access to its arguments, local variables and fields, and the possibility to replace the return value.
Extended attributes
Extending the UI puts the first three together: adding components, settings panels, threads and cleaning up on unload. Example plugin builds a small plugin from scratch.
ExtensionHasLocalization adds languages of the interface, ExtensionHasCss adds CSS to the pages.

Hooks are attached by class and method name and read local variables and fields by name. Renaming a method or a variable in the application silently disables the part of a plugin that used it (a warning is logged). Build plugins from the same source tree as the application they run in, and test them after every update. LingoLLM itself verifies the decorators of an extension before it starts it and refuses ones that ask for classes, methods, arguments, locals or fields that don't exist.

This page covers what every plugin needs: the Maven project, the bundle activator, the LingoLLMExtension and how LingoLLM loads, starts and unloads it.
A plugin is an ordinary Maven project with bundle packaging:
Use your own package; com.github.enerccio.lingollm.extensions is the application's (the LingoLLMExtension interface).

c:
myplugin/
├── pom.xml
└── src/main/java/com/example/lingollm/myplugin/
    ├── MyPluginActivator.java     BundleActivator - registers the extension
    ├── MyPluginExtension.java     LingoLLMExtension - registers hooks, cleans up
    ├── model/                     data classes stored as JSON in attributes (optional)
    ├── service/                   plugin logic, @Configurable (optional)
    └── ui/                        Vaadin components (optional)

p: The pom of a plugin follows the sketch below (lingollm/plugins/gemma4toolsfix/pom.xml is a complete one; Marginalia's plugins have the same shape). A plugin inside the repository would inherit its version from the parent POM (parent with lingollm-parent) and be a module of it; a plugin of your own outside the repository has no parent and gives its version itself. The important parts:

Everything from the application is provided. LingoLLM runs the bundle with boot delegation for all packages (see Class loading), so the bundle sees exactly the classes and libraries of the running WAR. Bundling your own copy of Vaadin, Spring or Gson would create a second, incompatible copy of their classes.

Versions must match the application. Take the Vaadin, Gson and commons versions from lingollm/pom.xml. Compiling against a different Vaadin version than the one that runs usually works until it doesn't.
Import-Package imports nothing. The single negated entry stops bnd from generating Import-Package headers - they are not needed with boot delegation and would make the bundle fail to resolve.

AspectJ weaves Spring's AnnotationBeanConfigurerAspect into the plugin's classes, so a plugin class annotated @Configurable gets its @Autowired fields injected from the application's Spring context, like the application's own UI classes (AspectJ weaving). Without it, those fields stay null.
Libraries the application doesn't have must be embedded in the bundle (Embed-Dependency) or shaded. Keep this to a minimum.

Build with mvn package; the result is target/artifactId-version.jar. The application must be installed in the local Maven repository first (mvn install -DskipTests in lingollm/), and reinstalled whenever you change classes the plugin uses.

c:
<packaging>bundle</packaging>

<dependencies>
    <!-- the application's classes, installed by `mvn install` in lingollm/ -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>io.github.enerccio</groupId>
        <artifactId>lingollm</artifactId>
        <version>1.0.0</version>
        <classifier>classes</classifier>
        <scope>provided</scope>
    </dependency>
    <!-- plus, all `provided`: org.apache.felix.framework, vaadin-core, and any library
         of the application you use directly (gson, commons-lang3, font-awesome-iron-iconset...) -->
</dependencies>

<build>
    <plugins>
        <!-- maven-compiler-plugin, release 25 -->
        <!-- aspectj-maven-plugin with spring-aspects as aspect library - needed for @Configurable -->
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.apache.felix</groupId>
            <artifactId>maven-bundle-plugin</artifactId>
            <version>6.2.0</version>
            <extensions>true</extensions>
            <configuration>
                <instructions>
                    <Bundle-SymbolicName>${project.artifactId}</Bundle-SymbolicName>
                    <Bundle-Version>${project.version}</Bundle-Version>
                    <Bundle-Activator>com.example.lingollm.myplugin.MyPluginActivator</Bundle-Activator>
                    <Import-Package>!com.example.lingollm.myplugin.*</Import-Package>
                    <Export-Package>com.example.lingollm.myplugin.*</Export-Package>
                </instructions>
            </configuration>
        </plugin>
    </plugins>
</build>

p: The bundle's activator registers one LingoLLMExtension as an OSGi service. That's all it should do - LingoLLM discovers the service and calls it:
Only bundles that register a LingoLLMExtension are listed in Admin → Extensions.

onExtensionLoad registers everything the plugin needs: decorators (extensionService.registerDecorator(...), see @Extendable hooks), cleanup contributors (Extended attributes). It should not build UI - there is no UI at that moment. UI is added later, from decorators, when the user opens the screen the plugin extends.

onExtensionUnload undoes all of it: unregister every decorator and listener, remove the components the plugin added to open screens (Unloading), stop background work. Nothing is removed automatically - a decorator left registered keeps running, from a bundle that no longer exists.
Annotate the extension @Configurable and inject what you need:

Any bean of the application can be injected - every service in domain/service (Services), Localization, InferenceServices, Configuration, OsgiService... Plugin classes created with new (services, dialogs, forms) can be @Configurable too; the example plugin creates its service object in the extension (new NotesService()) and it is injected the same way.

At startup onExtensionLoad runs without a UI, so UIUtils.internalServerError(...) (which opens a dialog) can't show anything. Throw instead: an exception that escapes onExtensionLoad is logged, onExtensionUnload is called to undo what was registered so far and the bundle is stopped. The other extensions load normally; an upload shows the error to the administrator.

Startup. OsgiServiceImpl listens for the root context's ContextRefreshedEvent, starts Felix with its storage in ~/.lingollm/extensions/org.eclipse.osgi (wiped on every start, so the JARs are always read fresh), installs every *.jar in ~/.lingollm/extensions and starts them. For each LingoLLMExtension service a bundle registered, it calls onExtensionLoad. Each JAR is installed and started on its own: one that can't be installed (not a bundle, a second copy of an installed plugin) or fails to start is logged with its file name and skipped. When the folder holds several versions of one extension (same symbolic name, e.g. an update copied next to the old JAR), only the newest is started; a warning names the skipped JARs, which are moved to extensions/old-versions (not deleted). Before a bundle is started it is verified: the decorators it registers are checked against this version of the application (Verification before loading). An invalid extension stays installed but is not started, and its report is logged. A bundle whose JAR has a jar name.STOPPED flag next to it (see Stopping) is installed but not started either.

Installing at runtime. Admin → Extensions → Load Extension (.jar) writes the uploaded file into ~/.lingollm/extensions (the file name is sanitized: only letters, digits, ., _ and -) and installs and starts it the same way, verification included (OsgiService.installPackage, like uninstallPackage administrators only: AdminGuard.requireAdmin(); an invalid upload throws ExtensionVerificationException with the report). Screens that are already open are not rebuilt: the plugin's decorators run the next time the decorated methods run (the next time the user selects a language profile, opens a tab...).

Updating. Uploading a bundle whose symbolic name (or file name) is already installed replaces it: the old one is unloaded as by Unload, uninstalled and its JAR deleted, then the new one is loaded. If the new one fails to install, verify or start, its JAR is deleted and the old one is put back.

Unloading. Unload calls the callbacks registered with bindAttachableComponent, then onExtensionUnload, uninstalls the bundle and deletes its JAR and its verification reports (OsgiService.uninstallPackage). Bundles that failed to start are listed too (state Installed or Resolved) and can be unloaded the same way.

Stopping. Stop (OsgiService.stopExtension, administrators only) creates the jar name.STOPPED flag file, unloads the extension like Unload does (bound callbacks, onExtensionUnload) and stops the bundle; the bundle stays installed and is listed with the state Stopped (isStopped). Start (startExtension) verifies it, starts it and deletes the flag; when that fails, the flag stays. The flag survives restarts. Uploading a replacement of a stopped extension deletes the flag, and Unload deletes the flag too.

Shutdown. When the application stops (the root context closes), every extension is unloaded the same way - bound callbacks, onExtensionUnload, the activator's stop - and the framework is stopped. Still save data as you go: a killed process runs none of this.

An extension should not use LoggerFactory (its lines are mixed with everything else and the administrator cannot see them next to the extension). OsgiService.createLogger(bundle) returns an org.slf4j.Logger that writes to its own file, jar name.log in the extensions folder (myplugin.jar.log), which administrators read in Admin → Extensions → Log:

The usual SLF4J API: {} placeholders and a trailing throwable (logged with its stack trace). TRACE is dropped, DEBUG and above are written. Each line has the time, level, thread, logger name (the symbolic name by default) and the message. The line is also chained to the application log (logger extension.name, same level, so the level settings of the application apply - the release build logs at INFO and keeps chat content out of its log, so don't log chat text above DEBUG).

The logger is thread safe and can be kept; the file is opened for every line, so nothing stays open after the extension is gone. A file over 2 MB is moved to jar name.log.old (replacing the previous one).
OsgiService.readLog(bundle, maxBytes) and clearLog(bundle) (administrators only) read the end of the file and delete it. The log is deleted with the extension when it is unloaded.

Code that is not created by the extension class (components made by new, services) needs the logger too: pass it on to your service or keep it in a static holder that is set in onExtensionLoad and reset in onExtensionUnload, with LoggerFactory as the fallback before and after.
The class org.slf4j.Logger comes from the application (boot delegation); if your bundle lists its Import-Package explicitly, include org.slf4j.

OsgiService reports single extensions that are loaded or unloaded to ExtensionListeners, for code that has to react to the extension set - the application itself uses it to keep the styles of extensions in the pages (Styles of a plugin):
extensionLoaded(bundle, extension) is called after onExtensionLoad returned. An extension whose load failed is never reported (and not as unloaded either); it is unloaded again as before.
extensionUnloaded(bundle, extension) is called after onExtensionUnload, for every extension that was reported as loaded: Unload, an update that replaces the bundle, the shutdown of the application.

The methods run on the thread that loads or unloads (an administrator's request, the startup), with no UI session. Change a UI through ui.access(...). An exception is logged and doesn't stop other listeners or the loading.

Listeners get no events for extensions that are loaded already. Subscribe first, then read getLoadedExtensions(); an extension loaded between the two is seen twice, so handle repeats (CssRegistry.attach does).

Optional interfaces. Besides LingoLLMExtension, the extension class can implement ExtensionHasCss (styles put into every page, see Styles of a plugin) and ExtensionHasLocalization (languages for the UI: OsgiServiceImpl registers the returned LocalizationBundles in Localization right after onExtensionLoad returned and removes them when the extension is unloaded; a language that already has a bundle is refused, English can't be replaced).
The older ExtensionObserver (addSubscriber) reports the start and stop of the whole framework, including the pauses during an upload or unload.

Felix is started with org.osgi.framework.bootdelegation=* and the framework class loader as the bundle parent, which is the web application's class loader. Every class a bundle asks for is therefore looked up in the application first: LingoLLM's own classes, Vaadin, Spring, Hibernate, Gson, everything in WEB-INF/lib. The consequences:
Plugins use the application's classes directly - no imports, no service lookups, instanceof and casts work.
A plugin can't override or replace a library of the application, and can't use a different version of one.

Plugins don't see each other's classes through imports either; if two plugins need to cooperate, do it through shared data (attributes) or through the application's components. A plugin that uses the objects of another one (which may be missing, or unloaded and installed again) finds it among OsgiService.getLoadedExtensions() by the name of its class and calls it by reflection, taking the types it needs from extension.getClass().getClassLoader(). Do not import its packages (Import-Package, DynamicImport-Package) or name its classes in your code: the wiring is to one revision of the other bundle, so after it is unloaded and installed again your bundle keeps the old classes and does not recognize the new objects, and the JVM remembers a class reference that failed to resolve (NoClassDefFoundError), so a reference used while the other bundle was missing keeps failing after it is installed.

The plugin's own classes are loaded by the bundle's class loader, so the class names you pass to registerDecorator must be those of the application's classes; a plugin's own classes are never instrumented.

Most of what a plugin does starts with a decorator: an object whose onMethodEnter and onMethodLeave run before and after a method of an application class. Any method of a class annotated @Extendable can be decorated, private ones included, and the decorator can read the method's arguments and local variables and change what the method returns. A decorator of a method that returns a value can replace the value in onMethodLeave. The decorators of a method form a chain in the order they were registered, sharing one current value:

What a method returns is read by its caller, and every plugin that replaces it is now a part of that. A change of the declared return type of an @Extendable method is a change of its public API, and a plugin that replaces the value with a type that no longer fits is refused at run time.

Plugins can't add tables or columns - there is no way to run their own Flyway migrations. Instead, every data entity carries a JSON object where a plugin can keep whatever it needs: ExtendableEntity.attributes. It is saved with the entity, loaded with it, and travels with it into backups.
All data entities extend ExtendableEntity (Domain model):

Typical plugin data

Per-profile state and settings - the example plugin keeps notes here.

Per-provider options. (LingoLLM itself keeps the per-user limits of a shared AI in the @ExtendedAttribute field AI.limits, see Domain model.)

Per-user plugin settings.

p: Use one top-level key per plugin, named after the plugin's package, and put a JSON tree of your own model classes under it. Follow this pattern:
Rules:
Save through the entity's service - save(...), not saveWithoutEvent(...). See How attributes are stored for why.

Load before you change. Entities held by the UI are detached copies, and the one you got from a decorator may be older than the database. Reload it (service.find(entity) or find(id)), change the attributes, save it, and use the returned object from then on. Saving an old copy overwrites changes made since - to the plugin's data and to the rest of the entity.
When several components edit parts of one JSON tree, each change should re-read the stored tree, change only its part and save it, not save a copy it loaded earlier.
Version your data. There are no migrations; if the format changes, read old formats too (a version field in your JSON tree makes this easy) and never fail on data you don't understand.

Keep it small. The whole JSON object is serialized on every save of the entity, and some entities are saved often - a chat message may be saved as it is edited. Megabytes of history in a message's attributes slow the save down; keep history in one place (the profile) rather than in every message.

Per user: settingService.getOrCreate(UserSetting.class) returns the current user's settings; store under your key, save with settingService.save(userSetting). To add the settings to the Settings screen, see Extending the UI → Settings panels.
Whole installation: AppSettings the same way, only administrators should change it.

On save (JpaExtendableRepository.save) it builds one JSON object: each @ExtendedAttribute field of the entity under its field name, as a string, and each key of attributes with the prefix attributes_.
On load (@PostLoad) and after every save it fills the fields and attributes back from that JSON.

Two things follow from this:
saveWithoutEvent (used by backup restore, which writes extendedContent directly) does not serialize: changes to attributes saved that way are lost. Always use save.
The _fulltext column that is written next to extendedContent is built only from the application's @Fulltextable fields. A plugin's attributes are not in it and can't be added to it.

@ExtendedAttribute is the application's own way of adding fields to an entity without a migration - many fields of Language, FreeChat, FreeChatMessage, AI and the settings are stored like this. It works for String, the numeric types, boolean, Date and enums, stored as strings (dates as ISO-8601 instants in UTC). @ExtendedAttribute(inject = true, injectPrefix = ...) on a JsonObject field (or a class, which is converted with Gson) spreads its keys with that prefix, which is how attributes itself is declared. p: Plugins add to the user interface from decorators: when a method that builds part of a screen runs, the plugin's decorator finds the component it built and adds to it. This page collects the patterns plugins use. Read @Extendable hooks first, and User interface for the conventions of the UI code.

Some screens exist twice: the desktop class and its phone twin (DesktopWorkspace and PhoneWorkspace, AIPart and PhoneAIPart), and a decorator only runs for the class it was registered for. Register it a second time for the phone class to support phones, or leave it out and the extension simply adds nothing there, see The phone twins. LanguagePart and UserPart are shared.
Find the component - a field, a local variable or an argument of the decorated method.

Add only once. Many methods run more than once for the same component (refresh(), UserPart.refresh...), so mark the component with ComponentUtil.setData(component, key, value) and check the mark first. Prefix the keys with your plugin's package (KEY + .menuItem, see Extended attributes) - the components are shared with the application and every other plugin.
Remember what you added, so that onExtensionUnload can remove it (Unloading).

Find the layout and insert at a position relative to a known child. LanguagePart.create() builds a VerticalLayout (local layout) with the language selector (local header) and the container of the language screen:

A component created once for a view must not hold on to things that change in it: LanguagePart stays the same when the user picks another profile, so a panel bound to the profile it was created with ends up acting on the wrong one. Look the current value up when it is needed, or hook the method that runs on every change (selectLanguage(language, remember) has the profile as its argument, showLanguage(language) rebuilds the screen of a language - the example plugin uses it).
DesktopWorkspace.create() builds the HTabSheet held by the field tabs. On leave a decorator can add a tab:

The tab is not a WorkspaceComponent of the workspace: it gets no refresh/onTabSwitched calls and is not disabled while the settings have unsaved changes, so keep it self-contained. Do the same for PhoneWorkspace, which has a drawer instead of a tab sheet (its tabs field is a Tabs, the content is shown with layout.setContent; read the class before you decorate it).

c:
HTabSheet tabs = context.getReflectiveFieldValue(instrumented, "tabs", HTabSheet.class);
Tab tab = tabs.add("My tab", myComponent);

p: A grid the part keeps in a field can get more columns. AIPart.create() builds grid, a GridAI; after it, add a button to every row and keep the column to remove it on unload:
The row's item is the entity itself; read the context that is not part of it from the part, not from the row.

The decorator can change any component the method built: read it from a local variable, a field or an argument and change it (a label, a style class, a tooltip). If more plugins change the same component, they run in the order they were loaded and the last one wins - append or prefix rather than replace where you can.
The Settings screen (UserPart) has an Extension Settings tab with an Accordion in the field extensionSettings, empty unless plugins add to it. A plugin uses two decorators:

Changes in the panel's fields are tracked like the application's own: any value change outside of UserPart.refresh (and its decorators) locks the workspace navigation until the user saves or discards. Fill the form in the refresh decorator, not later (e.g. from a background thread), or the loaded values count as changes.

Saving on enter lets the application's own settingService.save(userSetting) store the plugin's values too. Note that save() returns early when the application's own fields don't validate - then the plugin's values are not stored either.
Plugin dialogs and components are ordinary Vaadin classes in the bundle. Annotate them @Configurable to inject services. Follow the application's conventions (User interface → Conventions).
What plugins can't do:

Add frontend resources. The browser side of LingoLLM is one bundle built with the WAR. A plugin can use every Vaadin component and add-on the application already uses (Vaadin core components, the FontAwesome icons, Viritin's VTabSheet...), but @CssImport, @JsModule, @NpmPackage and add-ons with their own web components don't work from a plugin. Style with the classes of CssStyles (addClassName(CssStyles.TEXT_SECONDARY)), which the application's shared-styles.css defines. A style only your plugin uses goes into a CSS file in the bundle's src/main/resources that the application puts into the page for you (Styles of a plugin), with its class names as constants in the plugin. Use getStyle() only for a value known at runtime.

Add localization keys. Localization knows only the application's L keys. The bundled plugins use English strings; a plugin that wants translations of its own texts has to bring its own (a ResourceBundle in the bundle, chosen by Localization.getCurrentLanguage()). A plugin can add a language for the application's texts with ExtensionHasLocalization, see Plugin basics.
Add routes. Routes are registered when the servlet starts. Use dialogs and tabs instead.
A plugin can't add to the application's stylesheet, but it can ship its own CSS. Implement ExtensionHasCss on the class that implements LingoLLMExtension:

getCss returns the CSS text for a page, or null/blank when the extension has no styles there. The entry point is the root component of the page: Main (the workspace), which implements ApplicationEntryPoint. The text is usually a resource of the bundle, read once and cached:

Use Lumo variables (var(--lumo-contrast-10pct)) in the rules and keep the class names as constants next to the loader (a MyStyles class and my-plugin.css); prefix them with the plugin's name, the page is shared with the application and other plugins.
What the application does. The entry point owns a CssRegistry (created in onAttach, released in onDetach). For every UI it
adds the style of each extension that is loaded already when the entry point is attached (an extension loaded at startup, or before the user opened the page),
adds the style of an extension that is loaded while the page is open (Admin → Extensions → Load), so it works without a reload,
removes the style again when the extension is unloaded, replaced by a newer version or the application stops.

The CSS goes into a style id=lingollm-extension-css-extension class name element in the document head; the element is replaced if it exists, so nothing is added twice. The registry listens to OsgiService through an ExtensionListener (Extension events). getCss is called once per page and extension and an exception from it is logged and skips only that extension, but it should not do anything expensive.

Don't add the style element from your own components (executeJs in a constructor): the style would not be removed when the extension is unloaded and would be added again for each component. Return it from getCss.

Inside click listeners and other event handlers, catch exceptions and report them like the application does: UIUtils.internalServerError(loc, e) logs and shows an error dialog - pass an injected Localization. Expected problems go to Notification. Failures of the model API (InferenceException) are explained by UIUtils.inferenceError(loc, e) or, as text, InferenceErrors.messageOf(loc, e). Exceptions in decorators themselves are logged by the ExtensionService and don't need handling unless you want to show something.

Decorators run on the thread that called the decorated method. For UI methods that's a request thread holding the Vaadin session lock, so decorators can change components directly and services see the current user.

Anything slow - calling a model, large imports - belongs on another thread, with the same rules as in the application (Background work and push): capture UI.getCurrent() on the UI thread, change components only inside ui.access(...), push with UIPushGuard.push(ui), and wrap service calls that need the current user in the request scope.

InferenceServices.forAI(ai) returns the client for a provider: stream(...) and infer(...) send a list of messages and call back on another thread, with the limits and the usage of the user applied (Services → Inference). A plugin asks for a whole answer like this:

The callbacks run on a worker thread, so the UI is captured first and the component changes go through ui.access. An error of the provider arrives as an InferenceException, which UIUtils.inferenceError explains to the user. For a structured answer pass a class instead (infer(payload, MyAnswer.class, callback)), for function calls a FunctionSet.
When a plugin is unloaded, components it added to open screens stay there - with listeners pointing into a bundle that is gone - unless the plugin removes them. There are two ways.
Track and remove - keep the extended components in weak sets (so that closed screens can be garbage collected) and undo the changes in onExtensionUnload:

Bind a callback - OsgiService.bindAttachableComponent(component, callback, extension) registers callback to run when the extension is unloaded, for as long as component is attached (a component that is detached and attached again - moved, in a tab sheet, in a reopened dialog - stays bound):

(osgiService is the one passed to onExtensionLoad, or injected.) The callbacks run before onExtensionUnload, each inside ui.access(...) of its component's UI, so they can change the component directly. A component that is detached when the extension is unloaded runs its callback when it is attached again. Calling bindAttachableComponent for an extension that isn't loaded throws an IllegalStateException.

onExtensionUnload runs on the request thread of the administrator who clicked Unload, but the components belong to every user's open screens. Change them inside component.getUI().ifPresent(ui - ui.access(...)), as above, or with UIUtils.accessComponent(component, () - ...), which does the same and runs the change directly when the component isn't attached.

Data in attributes stays after unloading, so loading the plugin again picks up where it left off. If your plugin is uninstalled for good, its data stays in the database (and in backups) - harmless, but say so in its README.

test/llm/MockLLMServer is a small OpenAI-compatible server on 127.0.0.1 with a random port, built on the JDK's HttpServer. One shared server lives for the whole test JVM (MockLLMServer.shared()); each test gets its own scenario with its own base URL, http://127.0.0.1:port/scenario-id/v1. A provider created with createAI() points to the test's scenario, so tests never see each other's requests or answers.
It answers:
Endpoint
GET /models
The scenario's model list (default mock-model; change with llm.models(...)).
POST /chat/completions
Streaming (server-sent events) and non-streaming chat completions.
Chat completions are answered in this order:
queued responses - llm.enqueue(...) or llm.reply(text), one per request;
the responder function - llm.respondWith(request - ...), if set and it returns a response;
the fallback - llm.fallback(...);
otherwise HTTP 500 no response programmed.
MockLLMResponse builds one answer:
waitFor(latch) is the tool for "while generating" states: the request is received, the caller waits for the stream, and the test can cancel it or inspect the state before releasing the latch.

The openai-java client retries 408, 409, 429 and 5xx responses. A queued error response is consumed once per attempt, so enqueue it several times (or use fallback) when a test expects the error to reach LingoLLM. The server closes the connection after every response, so a retry never reuses a stale pooled connection.

c:
MockLLMResponse.text("Hello world")                        // one content chunk
MockLLMResponse.chunks("Hel", "lo").chunkDelay(ofMillis(50))
MockLLMResponse.split(longText, 20)                        // chunks of 20 characters
MockLLMResponse.text("answer").withReasoning("thinking")   // reasoning chunks first
MockLLMResponse.text("answer").withReasoning("...").reasoningField("reasoning")  // instead of reasoning_content
MockLLMResponse.text("cut").finishReason("length")
MockLLMResponse.error(429, "slow down")                    // OpenAI-style error body
MockLLMResponse.chunks("a", "b", "c").disconnectAfter(2)   // stream ends abruptly
MockLLMResponse.text("answer").usage(120, 8)               // token counts in the last chunk (only if asked for)
MockLLMResponse.text("late").waitFor(latch)                // held until the latch is released
MockLLMResponse.toolCall("add", "{\"a\":1}")               // the model calls a function; .andToolCall(...) adds one

Tests of failure paths make the code log errors on purpose. To keep them out of the test output (where they look like real failures) and to assert on them, capture the logger with test/ExpectedLog:

While the capture is open, the logger's events are recorded and not passed to the console; errors(), warnings() and atLeast(level) return the messages, entries() the full events with their exceptions.

ExtendableMethodVisitorTest transforms fixture classes from instruct/fixture/ with instruct/Instrumenter - the same transformation the agent applies, without an agent - and checks that the result verifies, keeps the class schema, behaves like the original and exposes arguments and locals to decorators.
RuntimeInstrumentationTest installs the real agent into the test JVM and checks classes loaded both before and after the installation (fixture/agent/).

ExtensionVerifierTest runs the extension verification on the extensions of fixture/verify/VerifyFixtures (decorators that are valid, ask for things that don't exist, or can't be followed) against the decorated VerifyTarget. Their class files are packed into a JAR on the fly and served by a stand-in Bundle. Decorators must be anonymous classes with the context calls inside them, as in a real extension - a decorator that delegates to a helper class would not be checked.

PublicAPISignatureTest checks the @PublicAPI of every instrumented method of every @Extendable class of the application against the compiled classes (target/classes). It reads them with ByteBuddy's type pool and the local variable table (PublicAPISignatures), so the application classes are not loaded or initialized, and it needs the classes compiled by ajc like the application. A failure names the method and prints the annotation the method needs.

The fixtures are compiled with the same -parameters and preserveAllLocals options as the application; if you change the compiler settings in pom.xml, these tests tell you whether extensions still see names of arguments and locals.

LingoLLM is built once as a WAR and then shipped in two forms: a Docker image for servers and a desktop app with its own Java runtime and Jetty. This page describes how each is built, what CI does, and how a release is made. For everyday builds see Building from source.

The WAR always runs in Vaadin production mode: build-frontend writes the production flow-build-info.json into it, and a development one left in src/main/resources is never packaged (see Development and production mode).

The build also needs the Git history: git-commit-id-plugin writes the commit id and the closest tag into git.properties, and the WAR filters them into its build info. Build from a clone, not from a source archive.

starts with docker-entrypoint.sh (as lingollm-entrypoint.sh) as root: it creates the data folder if needed and, when it isn't owned by jetty - a ./data bind mount that Docker created on a Linux host is owned by root - changes its owner to jetty (recursively, only then). DesktopLauncher is the main class of the app image and of the portable scripts. It depends on the JDK only and starts Jetty in its own JVM by loading start.jar through a class loader, so it never needs Jetty on the classpath and never ends up in the WAR. On start it:
resolves the data folder home/.lingollm (--home sets user.home) and redirects its output to .lingollm/desktop/logs/;
finds server/ next to or above the launcher JAR (jpackage places app content differently per OS);
checks the port (default 8765): if LingoLLM already runs there, it just opens the browser; if another program uses it, it picks a free port (unless --port was given);

writes a Jetty base into .lingollm/desktop/jetty-base/ (modules ee11-*, webapps/ROOT.xml pointing to the WAR, a persistent work folder) - so the installation itself can stay read-only, e.g. inside a signed app bundle;
starts Jetty on 127.0.0.1, waits up to three minutes for the start page, then shows the tray icon (or a small window where there is no system tray) and opens the browser.

The JVM options needed by the extension agent (-Djdk.attach.allowAttachSelf=true -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading, plus --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED for SQLite) are passed by jpackage --java-options and by the scripts in bin/. The scripts add LINGOLLM_JAVA_OPTS. Keep the three places in sync - the desktop.javaOptions property and both scripts. On macOS, -Dapple.awt.UIElement=true keeps the app out of the Dock; it lives only in the tray.
Command-line options are described in Desktop app.

jlink and jpackage only build for the platform they run on, so each operating system and CPU is built on its own machine. CI does this with a build matrix (below). Locally you get only your own platform.

If you add a dependency that needs a JDK module not in desktop.modules (a ClassNotFoundException or NoClassDefFoundError for a java.* / javax.* / jdk.* class in the desktop log only), add the module to the list. jdeps --print-module-deps on the WAR's libraries helps to find it.

The app images are not signed or notarized. macOS Gatekeeper and Windows SmartScreen warn on the first start; the Desktop app page tells users how to get past it. Signing would be added to the jpackage call (--mac-sign, --mac-signing-key-user-name...) and, for Windows, as a separate signtool step in CI.

p: The manual is part of the repository: Retype reads manual/ and writes the static site to docs/ (configured in retype.yml). GitHub Pages serves docs/ from the master branch, so the published manual changes when a commit with a new docs/ reaches master. Rebuild and commit docs/ in the same change as the sources - see Building the manual.

Contributions are welcome: bug reports, fixes, new features, extensions, and corrections to this manual. This page describes how to report a problem, how changes are made and what a pull request should contain.
LingoLLM is released under the MIT License. By contributing you agree that your contribution is released under the same license.
Open an issue on GitHub. For a bug, include:
what you did, what happened and what you expected;
the version (desktop app archive name, or the commit for a Docker server) and how you run it;
the inference provider type and model, if the problem is about a provider (never your API key);
the relevant part of the log - see Where are the logs?. Logs may contain chat text; remove what you don't want to share.
Security problems (access to other users' data, login, cookies) should not be reported in a public issue - contact the maintainer privately through GitHub first.
TODO.md is the list of planned work for the first release, ordered by priority. Items marked 🧩 are good candidates for an extension instead of a change to the core.

For anything larger than a small fix, open an issue (or comment on an existing one) first and describe what you plan. Some features belong in an extension rather than in the core - see Plugin development.
Read Architecture and the page about the area you are changing.
Set up the build and make sure mvn test passes on a clean checkout - see Building from source.
Fork the repository and create a branch from master with a short descriptive name (fix-profile-selector, german-exercises).
Make the change, with tests where the area is testable (see Testing).
Run mvn test in lingollm/. If you touched classes plugins use, build your plugins too.
Start LingoLLM and try the change in the browser - most of the application is UI, which the tests don't cover.
Update the manual if users or developers will notice the change (see Documentation).
Push and open a pull request against master.

CI runs the tests and builds the desktop app on all platforms for every pull request that changes lingollm/ (see Continuous integration). A pull request is merged when CI is green and the change has been reviewed.
Commit messages follow the style already in the history: one line, lowercase, starting with a verb in the imperative, class and method names in backticks, related changes separated by a semicolon:
Common verbs: add, fix, update, remove, refactor, rename, migrate, handle. Mention the issue number when the commit fixes one (... (#17)).

Keep commits focused - one fix or one step of a feature per commit, not a mix of a feature, a reformat and an unrelated fix. Don't commit generated or local files: target/, src/main/frontend/generated/, src/main/bundles/, flow-build-info.json in src/main/resources and .idea/ are ignored by Git for this reason.

p: A good pull request:
does one thing, and says in the description what changed and why, with the issue it fixes;
for a UI change, includes a screenshot or a short description of what to click to see it;
adds or updates tests where it can, and passes mvn test;
adds a Flyway migration for every entity change (see Database & migrations) - never edit a migration that is already in master;
updates the manual;
doesn't change formatting of code it doesn't otherwise touch.
There is no formatter configuration in the repository; match the code around your change. In short:
Java 25. Modern language features (records, switch expressions, pattern matching, text blocks, var where the type is obvious) are welcome.
4 spaces, no tabs; opening braces on the same line; lines up to about 120 characters.
Javadoc on classes and on public methods whose purpose isn't obvious from the name. Write why and the contract (what null means, which thread, which transaction), not a restatement of the signature.

Logging through SLF4J (private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(X.class)), with {} placeholders. Chat content and prompts are logged at DEBUG only; API keys and passwords never. Plugins don't use LoggerFactory: they take the logger from OsgiService.createLogger(bundle) so their lines reach the extension log (Logging).
Return null for "not found" where the existing service API does (find, findForUser), and keep that consistent within a class.

An inference provider is AI, a language profile is Language (the language of the interface is loc.Language, a learnable language template Languages). Use the user-facing words (inference provider, language profile) in UI text, the manual and log messages.
Services are an interface in domain/service and an implementation NameImpl in domain/service/impl, registered in the Spring XML (see Services).
UI classes: a tab of the workspace is NamePart, the screens of a learnable language live in ui/lang/languages, a dialog is NameDialog, a reusable component in ui/components or ui/widgets.
Transactions live on services (@CommonTx, @CommonTxReadOnly), never on UI classes. Entities held by the UI are detached; reload them through the service before changing them.
The current user comes from the session-scoped User bean; services check ownership (findForUser) - the UI must not be the only thing protecting other users' data.

UI text is never hard-coded: add a key to loc/L.java and the text to loc/LocalizationBundleEN.java (and to the bundles of other languages, if any; a language without the key shows the English text), and use loc.getValue(L.KEY) (see User interface).
Threads: long work runs off the UI thread, and UI updates go through ui.access(...) (see Background work and push).

Extension points: methods that extensions decorate are @Extendable, and each of them declares its signature with @PublicAPI (PublicAPISignatureTest fails when a method has none or the annotation is out of date). Renaming or removing such a method, its parameters or its local variables breaks plugins - update the annotation, check the plugins you know of and mention the change in the pull request (see The public API and Keeping hooks working).
Schema: every entity change comes with a migration; Hibernate only validates the schema.
Use JUnit Jupiter and AssertJ, the test bases and the fake LLM server; no real network calls. See the checklist for a new test.
The manual you are reading is in manual/ (Markdown for Retype); docs/ is the generated site.
Change the Markdown in manual/, then run retype build and commit docs/ in the same pull request. Never edit files in docs/ by hand.
Preview with retype start.

Write for the reader of that part: the User guide talks about what users see and click (UI names in italics, no class names), the developer guide about code (paths relative to the main package, class names in backticks).
Screenshots go to manual/images/ (there are none yet). Diagrams are Mermaid code blocks, not images.
A screenshot that shows a third-party picture needs a credit on the Credits page (author, source, license, changes), and must be shared under the license of the picture.

Every developer page has verified (the commit it was last checked against the code; a page gets it with the first --stamp) and covers (the code it describes) in its front matter. python3 tools/check_dev_docs.py lists the pages whose covered code changed since then (-v names modified files, --check fails when any page is behind). After you review a page, mark it with --stamp page.md in a commit of its own. When a page starts describing other code, extend its covers.
Bugs you find while writing documentation are reported as an issue (see Reporting bugs and ideas).

New features that not every user needs - and anything experimental - are often better as an extension than as a change to the core. An extension can be developed and released on its own, and doesn't need a pull request at all. If you want it bundled with LingoLLM in lingollm/plugins/, open an issue first. See Plugin development and the example plugin.
